articles.title: Wall Street Issues Credit Warnings as AI Capex Demands Accelerate
articles.content: The seemingly endless gusher of capital that’s been showered on Silicon Valley during the AI boom may be coming to an end soon as Wall Street pushes back on massive spending plans. Recommended Video Following a brutal selloff in tech stocks over the past week, OpenAI slashed the target on its latest fundraising round to $20 billion from $30 billion, sources told the Financial Times . That also cut its expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion. The funding round was also upstaged by Anthropic, according to the report, as OpenAI’s arch-rival prepares to go public next month. Ahead of its IPO, Anthropic filed an S-1 on Monday that showed revenue has soared and its cash flow turned positive in the first half of this year. OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The timing couldn’t have been worse. Quarterly earnings reports from hyperscalers this week spooked investors. Alphabet saw its cash flow sink deeper into negative territory in the third quarter, with the Google parent also joining Meta and Amazon in charging ahead with massive spending plans. On Thursday, Alphabet fell about 12%, its worst day on record. To be sure, there were other positive signs as well, in addition to Anthropic’s bullish S-1. Microsoft reported strong cloud growth and stayed cash flow positive, though it said its capital spending will accelerate, while AI chip maker SK Hynix blew away earnings forecasts. But the narrative had already turned bearish, especially after AI debt fears sent shares and bonds of “neocloud” companies tumbling earlier this month. At the same time, OpenAI was seeking more capital just as other AI giants tapped financial markets heavily. This past week alone, Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in a bond sale. The prospect of hyperscalers continuing to hemorrhage funds was too much for S&P Global, which cut its outlook on Meta to “negative” from “stable” late Friday, citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around capital expenditure ​plans. The credit ratings agency maintained Meta at AA- but warned ⁠the social media leader’s leverage could top 1.0x as soon as 2027, which is the downgrade threshold for the current rating. That’s up from about 0.1x in 2025 and primarily reflects its strategy of leasing data center capacity rather than from its debt issuance. Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta’s capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there. As a result, it expects free operating cash flow to remain negative: -$22 billion this year, -$71 billion in 2027, and -$39 billion in 2028. Of course, other hyperscalers are spending heavily and running cash deficits, but S&P also said Meta’s ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers. “While we believe the company intends to monetize these investments via improved advertising tools that support faster ad revenue growth, as well as from the development of new revenue streams stemming from its introduction of agentic apps such as Muse, it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years,” S&P said. Meta’s rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added. In a statement to Fortune , a Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with S&P’s assessment of its AI monetization capabilities, pointing to “significant product and business opportunities” ahead. “Meta is already delivering stronger engagement, better recommendations, and greater returns for businesses as a result of AI investments,” the spokesperson continued. “We believe the technology and infrastructure we’re building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone.” The bearish environment on Wall Street also comes as rising bond yields have sent borrowing costs sharply higher, the political backlash against data centers is expected to help Democrats retake Congress, and the Iran war could re-escalate after midterm elections. Still, some bullish voices aren’t convinced the AI boom is about to go bust, and even think some retrenchment is a good thing . According to market veteran Ed Yardeni, the AI investment boom faces financial, physical, and political constraints. If any of these constraints worsen, stocks could dive further, especially considering that AI is now a major driver of corporate earnings and GDP growth, he said in a note this week. “However, we view these constraints as healthy for the durability of the AI boom!” he added. For example, if the supply of capital doesn’t flow as easily, it could lead to more efficient allocation, lowering the risk of overinvestment. Yardeni expects hyperscalers to retain access to financing—thanks to their strong balance sheets—and keep spending. In his view, it all comes down to the U.S. economy, which he said has performed remarkably well over the past few decades. Even the midterm elections are unlikely to derail it, regardless of which party controls Congress. “Further AI jitters therefore could set up buying opportunities rather than signal the end of the boom,” he said. articles.title: Seoul Viosys Eliminates Rare Earths from Advanced Semiconductor Emitters
articles.content: For three decades, white LEDs have depended on rare-earth materials such as yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG) layered onto a blue LED chip (Figure 1). Opto-semiconductor device maker Seoul Viosys Co Ltd (SVC) says that it has now broken that dependence by developing and mass producing a chip that emits white light without rare earths. The chip can be as small as 10µm. Seoul Viosys and its parent company South Korean LED maker Seoul Semiconductor Co Ltd opened up the micro-LED market with WICOP (Wafer Integrated Chip on PCB), which is a chip architecture that eliminates the package altogether. With WICOP, the two companies have already developed and mass produced ultraviolet, blue, green, red and infrared LEDs smaller than 100µm in size. WICOP 3 is the third generation of the technology, extending that capability to white light without rare-earth elements (REEs). White LEDs comprise about $10bn of the $15bn global market for packaged LEDs. WICOP 3 can now replace them with a technology free of rare earths, reckons the firm. More significantly, WICOP 3 is claimed to be the world’s first white opto-semiconductor to achieve white light in a micro-LED smaller than 100µm. WICOP 3 uses neither rare earths (a major source of environmental pollution) nor a package. Nor does it contain synthetic silicone resins, plastics or lead frames used in conventional LEDs. The result is said to be a far more environmentally friendly product that costs about half as much to make as a conventional white LED. The miniaturized transistor replaced the vacuum tube and created vast new markets in electronics. The company believes micro white opto-semiconductors can do the same. WICOP 3 generates white light from gallium nitride (GaN) alone. Also, the chip contains no plastics, silicone or other synthetic organic materials. It can hence last for decades. In lighting, invisible micro-emitters could be embedded in wallpaper or window glass, lighting a space with no fixtures at all. This would end the inconvenience of replacing bulbs and the high cost of fixtures. The company expects this to create a new market tens of times larger than today's $10bn white LED market. In its first mass production, a micro-LED chip measuring just 25µm x 10µm produced 0.015lm of white light. Its chromaticity falls inside the CIE standard white region (Figure 2). Luminous efficacy is already close to 100lm/W. The company aims to reach 200lm/W within two years. A conventional 1000µm x 1000µm chip achieves 50lm. Up to now, WICOP could make chips smaller, but white light still required a package containing rare earths. White chips therefore could not go below 1000µm. This held back cost reduction. White micro LEDs under 100µm (0.1mm) were also out of reach. Removing rare earths changes that. White light is now possible both in large chips of 1000µm and above and in micro LEDs below 100µm. Seoul Group (consisting of Seoul Semiconductor and Seoul Viosys) will start mass production of WICOP 3 in fourth-quarter 2026. It says it will supply first those customers that have respected its intellectual property and relied on its products. Seoul Viosys uses WICOP to produce micro-emitters smaller than 100µm. Micro-LEDs built on WICOP can now carry high volumes of AI data over distances from under 1cm to tens of meters. Over short distances, data has long traveled electrically through copper wire. Under the data loads of the AI era, copper links slow down, generate heat and consume much more power. Using light instead, Seoul Viosys arranges 1000 WICOP chips of about 10µm each in a grid within an area of 1mm2 or less. This array transmits data 10 times faster at one tenth of the power. Market research firms including Omdia forecast that this technology and augmented reality (AR) together will create a new $60bn market within five years (equal to half of today's DRAM memory market). Seoul Semiconductor’s founder Chung Hoon Lee says that the company intends to target WICOP 1, 2 and 3 at applications in AR glasses and AI data communications. These technologies work on scales of 10µm or less. To that end, it is seeking trusted upstream and downstream micro-LED supply chain partners in AR displays and AI transmitters. articles.title: Hong Kong Abandons Technopole Ambitions To Build University Town
articles.content: Government ministers, academics, and business leaders gathered at a Hong Kong auditorium for a two-day summit last week to discuss an ambitious project: building three universities towns in a sprawling area near the city’s border with mainland China. This aerial photo shows the construction site of the Hung Shui Kiu MTR station, October 30, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Hong Kong is betting on the multibillion-dollar Northern Metropolis project, which is set to transform about 300 square kilometres – roughly a third of the city’s territory – into an innovation and technology hub. Authorities hope that the project will power the city’s future growth and further integrate it into China’s Greater Bay Area, a region encompassing nine mainland municipalities plus the Special Administrative Regions of Hong Kong and Macau. “The main focus of its development will be its three university towns,” Chief Executive John Lee told the audience at last week’s summit, referring to the planned clusters at San Tin, Hung Shui Kiu, and Ta Kwu Ling. “They will be developed to band together five elements: education, technology, industry, talent, and city development,” Lee said. But university towns have not always been the main focus of the Northern Metropolis. In fact, when the mega-project was first announced in 2021 by Lee’s predecessor, Carrie Lam, the crown jewel was supposed to be a high-tech hub known as the San Tin Technopole. For years, the Northern Metropolis project was planned around the San Tin Technopole, which innovation chief Sun Dong projected could provide nearly half of the mega-development’s 650,000 promised new jobs. Earlier plans envisioned one university town near San Tin, not three. Lee noted the shift as well. “At the 2024 summit, I mentioned that we had set aside more than 80 hectares of land in the Northern Metropolis for a new University Town,” he said at the summit last week. “Our ambitions have only grown since then.” A two-day “Global University” summit is held in Hong Kong in late October 2026, as city leader John Lee seeks to woo international academics about Hong Kong’s plan to build three university towns in its sprawling Northern Metropolis. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. According to the latest strategy outlined in the government’s Five-Year Plan in September, the Northern Metropolis will host three university towns occupying a total area of more than 1,000 hectares. Among them, the Hung Shui Kiu campus is set to welcome its first institutions next year. Over the course of the project, “new concepts emerge every year or two that appear to redefine the whole Northern Metropolis,” said Chan Kim-ching of Liber Research Community. “The government used to say… innovation would be the main driver [of growth], but now it seems to be saying that education is the main driver of innovation,” Chan told HKFP in Cantonese. The pivot to university towns, however, may represent a more “realistic approach,” Chan added, pointing to the city’s high-calibre universities that already draw students from across Asia and have remained fiscally strong amid a period of general economic downturn. A banner shows the new development area in Ngau Tam Mei, where one of the campus areas of the San Tin University Town will be located, October 30, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The idea of developing Hong Kong’s vast frontier with Shenzhen has long featured in government policy – and was once a deeply contentious matter in the 2010s. In 2014, protesters and opposition politicians fiercely opposed a bill to allocate funding for what was then known as the Northeast New Territories New Development Areas plan. In June that year, affected residents and activists stormed the legislature while pan-democratic lawmakers filibustered over the bill inside the chamber, but the bill was passed nonetheless. However, with public dissent and the political opposition largely snuffed out after Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020 in the wake of the 2019 protests and unrest, there has been virtually no open opposition to the Northern Metropolis project. When Lam’s administration proposed the project in 2021, the San Tin Technopole was envisioned as its core. Authorities explicitly pitched the tech hub as Hong Kong’s Silicon Valley. An excavator is working at the Kwu Tung construction site, October 16, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. “The very announcement of the Northern Metropolis was itself a mutation [from pre-2021 policies],” said Liber’s Chan. “Even now, the project is still mutating, still evolving.” In the years following 2021, new concepts emerged, such as the “four zones” of the Metropolis: a “high-end professional services and logistics hub,” an “innovation and technology zone,” a “boundary commerce and industry zone,” and a “blue and green recreation, tourism and conservation circle.” Throughout this period, development remained centred on the San Tin Technopole. The government first mentioned that land would be reserved to build a “Northern Metropolis University Town” in 2023. Then, in his 2025 Policy Address, Chief Executive John Lee announced that the government would set up a working group on the planning and construction of the university town, which would be led by Chief Secretary Eric Chan. A government illustration showing the locations of the three planned university towns in Northern Metropolis. Photo: Screenshot, via GovHK. Lee added that the government was considering three potential sites, thus laying the groundwork for the current plan to develop three university towns instead of one. Chan said the previous Technopole-centric plan had been criticised for potentially overlapping with existing innovation and technology hubs in the city. “Is [the San Tin Technopole] just another Hong Kong Science Park?” Chan said, referring to the Pak Shek Kok tech hub that has been developed from the early 2000s. “You also have Cyberport [in Southern District].” “And there are hundreds of innovation hubs in the mainland, so what really is the relevance [of San Tin Technopole]?” Chan added. Chan Kim-ching (left) and Sunny Leung (right) of Liber Research Community. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The government’s approach has been to pitch the planned Technopole by offering various policy incentives to expedite its development. A dedicated Northern Metropolis Development Bill is currently in the legislative process. When passed, it will “streamline” the city’s urban planning and construction processes and facilitate cross-boundary flows of people and goods. Chan warned, however, that as with government-led development schemes worldwide, the ultimate test remains whether there is sufficient real-world demand to underpin the project’s ambitions. “Deregulation doesn’t necessarily lead to acceleration,” he said. “Acceleration hinges on whether there is effective demand to drive the plan.” A government illustration showing the projected Northern Metropolis. Photo: Screenshot. This year, early signs suggest that demand for the mega-project is cooler than authorities had hoped. In August, the government announced that a HK$1.03 billion tender for a pilot project in the Metropolis – the first of its kind – had been awarded to a consortium of six firms, which included Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com but lacked other major Chinese tech players. That same month, the Northern Metropolis’s first residential launch, Wheelock Properties’ Park Silicon in Kwu Tung, drew a lukewarm reception, offloading only 56 of the 100 units on offer on its opening day. Against this backdrop, pivoting to university towns as the driving force of the mega-project could prove a pragmatic move, Chan said. Five of Hong Kong’s eight publicly funded universities rank among the world’s top 100, and internationalised higher education has long been a key strength of the former British colony, even compared to China’s fast-growing cities. Nancy Ip, president of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, speaks during the Global University summit in late October, 2026. HKUST has committed to moving its medical school – the third in Hong Kong and currently under construction – into the Northern Metropolis. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The universities are also actively expanding and snapping up land in the city, thanks to the persistent demand from students from mainland China and across the region, driving up the institutions’ revenues in recent years. As of early 2025, the eight universities funded by the University Grants Committee had total reserves of nearly HK$140 billion, according to the South China Morning Post. The government has also increased the non-local student quota at universities, and the influx of mainland and international students is projected to continue growing. “The universities have huge demand for new campuses and student accommodation,” Chan said. “In fact, they are practically the only public bodies still expanding while the Hong Kong government is grappling with a fiscal deficit.” This aerial photo shows the demolition of Yik Yuen Tsuen, a village near the future Hung Shui Kiu MTR station, October 30, 2026. On the top right corner of the photo shows a large area planned for the campus area of the Hung Shui Kiu University Town. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. “So you are seeing the government leverage [the universities’] resources to power up the Northern Metropolis development,” he said. The pivot comes with its own set of challenges, Chan said, noting that Hong Kong’s idea of a university town is largely modelled after those in mainland China. In neighbouring Shenzhen, the Xili Lake International Science and Education City spans nearly 70 square kilometres – or 7,000 hectares, seven times the size of all Hong Kong’s proposed university towns combined. Elite mainland institutions, including Peking University and Tsinghua University, have established postgraduate divisions in the area alongside local Shenzhen campuses. The Xili Lake campuses sit only around 13 kilometres from Hong Kong’s San Tin. University towns in Hong Kong will have to avoid simply aping what Shenzhen has been doing in order to stay competitive, Chan said. But how to achieve that remained vague. Tracts of land that will soon become Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis, pictured with the Shenzhen skyline in the background on October 13, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Another danger of the current strategy is the risk of “over-planning,” Chan added, which could trigger cutthroat competition among the three university towns. “If, for example, you only need one town but end up building three, developers will naturally worry about a race to the bottom.” The government has outlined separate functions for the three planned towns. The Hung Shui Kiu site has been positioned as a “cultivation centre for smart manufacturing.” The San Tin University Town will focus on medicine, life technology, artificial intelligence and robotics, while the Ta Kwu Ling location will incorporate arts and “blue-green development elements.” But Chan said that it remained unclear how the university towns would create “synergy” among institutions, while Sunny Leung, another researcher with Liber, questioned whether the three clusters could generate sufficient revenue to sustain long-term development. Chan said Hong Kong is best positioned to leverage its strong international ties to attract overseas universities to partner with local institutions in the Northern Metropolis. Last week’s summit echoed Chan’s point, with speakers coming from 21 countries across the globe. Workers clear overgrowth from a construction site in Ha Tsuen, near Hung Shui Kiu – part of the planned Northern Metropolis – on October 16, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Yet, with geopolitical tensions rising and the China-US rivalry intensifying, it raises questions about how many Western institutions are willing to invest in Hong Kong, Chan noted. “Internationalisation will be hit by geopolitics. Which universities are willing to place the core of their research efforts in partnership with Hong Kong? articles.title: Automated Synthetic Misogyny Outpaces Modern Safety Legislation
articles.content: The current alarm about the future dangers of agentic AI might distract us from the very real AI harms already happening. As we speculate about whether machines might one day become dangerous to humankind, AI is deepening misogyny, eroding safety and automating gendered abuse. By Janine Deselaers and Janet Heard 1 Nov 2026 0 Photo:( iStock) Graphic: (Jocelyn Adamson) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper , short for "opposite the editorial page". Op-Eds allow authors who are not part of Daily Maverick's team of journalists to express opinions, perspectives and arguments on various issues of public interest. The views expressed are those of the author/authors and do not necessarily represent the views supported by Daily Maverick. Debate about “agentic AI”, systems that act independently and might go “rogue”, has prompted fresh calls for a pause in the AI race. But AI harms aren’t hypothetical, and the panic fostered by Big Tech founders themselves may be a distraction.  Timnit Gebru, the founder of the Distributed AI Research Institute, argues that AI companies stir up extinction fears to avoid discussing AI’s real harms , such as the ecological cost of data centres and autonomous weapons. We would add one more concern to her list: the intensifying violence against women and people of diverse sexual orientations, gender identities and expressions. Online and offline violence are still often treated as separate. However, harmful ideas that circulate across social media at speed, shaping attitudes about women, masculinity and entitlement, do not remain online. They spill over into offline stalking, harassment, intimidation and physical violence. Research, including a UN Women report , shows that violence against women is “rooted in gender inequality and discrimination, unequal power relations, and harmful social norms”, and that femicide is its most extreme manifestation." The recent murders of nine women within months in Ekurhuleni, Gauteng, prompted Amnesty International South Africa to call on the state to recognise femicid e   as a distinct crime. Research confirms that norms around gender equality play a significant role in driving intimate partner femicide. These norms are increasingly shaped on social media and in the so-called manosphere , a loose network of right-leaning online spaces promoting misogynistic narratives, popularised by influencers such as Andrew Tate, and spreading across Africa . So how does AI play into all of this? AI is changing the scale of gendered harms, as a new r esearch report by the Association for Progressive Communications notes.  “Coordinated harassment campaigns or gender disinformation campaigns before maybe would have required an organised human effort that now can be run at volumes and with a persistence that was simply either not possible before or [was] very costly,” says author Daniela Schnidrig. AI also lowers the technical threshold for abuse. Generative AI can now produce sexualised content from a single photo, and the majority of victims of sexually explicit deepfakes are women and gender-diverse persons . A 2025 study by the Oxford Internet Institute identified nearly 35,000 publicly downloadable deepfake model variants and found that 96% of those analysed targeted identifiable women. The infrastructure itself is not neutral either. AI systems learn from training data that reproduces harmful stereotypes and racist ideas, as gender studies professor Safiya Umoja Noble demonstrated as early as 2018 in Algorithms of Oppression .  Social media and AI are increasingly bound together in a closed loop, as content is generated by AI, amplified by AI-driven algorithms and moderated by AI. These engagement-optimised algorithms push sensational material, while automated tools fail to recognise gendered harm, especially in Global South contexts. With only 22% of the world’s AI professionals being women and hardly any women leading major social media companies, standards are shaped by those who have historically defined what counts as harm, rather than by those who bear the brunt of abuse.  Double standards Years after the breastfeeding censorship debate, Meta’s “Nudity and sexual activity” guidelines still restrict images of female nipples but not male ones, a rule whose cultural and health harms range from the automated removal of photos of Himba women in traditional attire in 2024 (a ban that was subsequently overturned), to the flagging of restorative nipple tattoos for breast cancer survivors, as reported in June this year by the BBC . Double standards are at play. While AI-generated, non-consensual images remain online, platforms shadow-ban content by women and LGBTQIA+ people, hiding their posts without warning, with activists particularly targeted . This abuse drives women out of public life. A UN Women study found that 70% of women journalists, activists and human rights defenders surveyed had experienced online violence, and nearly one in four had faced AI-assisted abuse. Consequences range from self-censorship on social media and at work to severe mental health impacts, including anxiety and depression. Solutions do not require rejecting technology. AI offers real opportunities to support survivors and to strengthen the institutions meant to protect them. Chatbots like Zuzi offer survivor-centred information on gender-based violence in local languages such as isiZulu, while the FemAI Policy Playbook by Stellenbosch University’s Policy Innovation Lab shows how AI could connect fragmented data across police, health and justice institutions so that a survivor’s journey through the system can be followed and failures in support identified.  The profit motive But the answer is not an abstract slowdown of AI development. A redesign of power structures is required. We must ask why content that fuels GBV is amplified in the first place, and ultimately, the answer is money. Under digital economist Nick Srnicek’s “ Platform Capitalism ”, companies profit from engagement, and misogyny generates plenty of it,  turning hate into revenue through algorithms and marketing schemes. Recent studies support this. Regulation that focuses on content removal while leaving these hugely profitable revenue models untouched will fall short. Accountability measures, such as interrupting revenue streams and algorithmic auditing,  deserve attention. Gender perspectives and harm analysis must be built into AI policy from the start, with those affected by digital abuse represented in the design, regulation and evaluation of these systems. Regulation must also be contextual, and international frameworks must give countries the sovereignty to regulate tech giants and reclaim public spaces.  Guidelines ignoring Global South realities will not work. While the African Union’s 2024 Continental AI Strategy names Technology-Facilitated GBV as a risk, a commentary for the European Centre for Development Policy Management notes that AU digital policies do not adequately embed gender equality into operational design. With much AI policy still to be written, initiatives like Pollicy’s Afro-feminist handbook and the Feminist AI Research Network show what gender-just governance could look like.  The stakes are high. If these harms go unaddressed, we risk backsliding on decades of hard-won intersectional justice gains. The debate over a “pause” should force a more honest question, not whether harm could arrive someday, but why so much of it is already here and why those most affected are still being asked to wait. Järjestelmään kuulumisesta kerrotaan esimerkiksi verkkokaupan toimitusehdoissa. Tullin käsittelymaksu on eri asia kuin Postin käsittelymaksu, joka täytyy maksaa, jos Posti kuljettaa paketin ja jos tavarasta on maksettava tullauksen yhteydessä maahantuontiveroja. To better track incidents of smoking or burning power banks across different types of transportation, the board on May 26 asked the Ministry of Transportation and Communications and transportation authorities in Taipei, New Taipei City, Taoyuan, Taichung and Kaohsiung to provide data on such incidents. From 2024 to June, 17 incidents of power banks smoking or catching fire were recorded, including nine last year, according to the data, which covered aircraft, boats, rail and commercial motor vehicles. Twelve incidents occurred on railways, the highest among transportation modes, it showed. Seven incidents caused equipment damage to vehicles, mostly to seats and flooring. The status of the power bank was not known in the nine other incidents. articles.title: Enterprise Knowledge Lacks Algorithmic Anchor for Production
articles.content: Let’s try a little thought experiment in technology-fiction: what would have happened if Larry Page and Sergey Brin’s PageRank , back in 1998, had failed to attract its first investors? Google didn’t invent the search engine: there were plenty of them before, from AltaVista, Excite, Lycos or others who were counting words on pages and selling their results page to the highest bidder, to catalog or portal concepts such as Yahoo! or AOL, that attempted to capture the users’ attention as much as they could to be able to serve them advertising, the more the better. Imagine if these concepts would have gone the distance, and deprived us of the web that resulted from Google’s easy and efficient way of searching … What did Larry Page and Sergey Brin realize? They adapted and extended the citation index (or its consequence, the citation impact ), a system that they knew worked for academic literature (remember, these guys were graduate students working on their Ph.D., and thus reading academic papers like there was no tomorrow!), and moved it into a new context: the web. They realized there was an underused signal, relationships among pages, and used it to generate a metric, weighting links according to the importance of the pages providing them, that not only allowed them to index the web, but also to define attention as a social construct: a page is important when other pages link to it with a certain term. As I’ve said several times, corporate AI is completely different from individual AI : companies don’t need just answers to questions, what they need is persistent memory and state, feedback learning loops, embedded cybersecurity, logs that can be tracked and not manipulated , etc. So far, companies are building these required scaffolding using twentieth-century tools such as Python, and AI agents are proving to be smart enough as to escape from these containments and do all sort of bad things — not because they are intrinsically evil (they cannot be), but because the goals and the guardrails are badly defined, or due to excessive permissions, prompt injection, or weak isolation. These companies are trying to define these properties by repeatedly assembling application by application, rather than supplied coherently by the platform. However, companies are repeatedly making all sorts of decisions about suppliers, customers, inventory, pricing, service, etc. Those decisions are constantly generating evidence of what works and what not, provided that the company is smart enough to capture them. What if we could evaluate AI by whether the company learns and improves, beyond the quality of individual outputs? What if AI optimization becomes more important than having access to bigger models ? A company does not just need a very powerful AI model: it needs an architecture that coordinates capabilities toward its goals. Researchers writing on Berkeley’s AI research blog explicitly describe the shift toward compound AI systems , where system design can offer better returns than further model scaling. Other experiments, such as FrugalGPT or DSPy are specific precedents for making model selection subordinate to results: FrugalGPT demonstrated that model cascades can match the strongest individual model with up to 98% lower cost on its evaluated tasks, and DSPy showed that optimized pipelines using smaller models can compete with approaches using much larger proprietary models. What makes the next step consequential? The ability to learn across executions. If we manage to make each interaction inform subsequent decisions across the relevant population, we can achieve a substantial advantage. And world models add precisely this possibility: they can anticipate consequences before acting. Research about Dreamer successfully demonstrates this mechanism across diverse control tasks . And once you have that, you can use reinforcement learning or another optimization mechanism uses experience to progressively improve decisions. While broadly available models available through commercial APIs or open-weight deployments can provide shared capabilities, company-specific experience can produce truly differentiated decisions, the ones that can really make the difference. Imagine, for instance, the renewal decisions you can make when you can learn from observed retention outcomes. However, bear in mind that simple accumulation does not automatically guarantee an advantage : you have to process the information properly, but not “with an AI”… with “your AI”. Make sure you put the training in the correct layer, the one you can administer and control. PageRank unlocked value in something the web was already producing: links. The next breakthrough in corporate AI could unlock value in something companies already produce every day: experience. If that experience becomes accumulated learning that the company controls and retains as models change, the competitive advantage starts to belong to the business itself. The company that stopped waiting for a smarter model might simply be the first to realize that its most valuable intelligence is the intelligence it learns to build — and keep. My proposed buying criterion is based on the following question: can the company replace its model provider while retaining its operational history, learned policies, objectives and demonstrated gains? Can your company export and reuse that learning when changing platform providers? Do you own your corporate intelligence , or do you rent the whole thing? When you stop working with “vanilla AI” and you start working with “your own AI”, you control the learning asset, without requiring ownership of every underlying model. And that’s when you can become a truly optimizable company . Basically, optimization, not a bigger model, is what you need. articles.title: Meta Creative Engine Threatens Commercial Advertising Agencies
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks , is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average. Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents. Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.” While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.” The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added. Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet. Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset. Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them. and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents. Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said. Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email. There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement. Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent . But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.

articles.title: Indian Digital Governance Stalls Over Unresolved Telecom Surveillance Inquiries
articles.content: Welcome to our special edition newsletter, dedicated to the important questions we asked authorities and relevant stakeholders throughout October. Despite receiving either no response or only generic replies that barely scratched the surface, we believe these questions are crucial and deserve to be brought to your attention. First, an invitation. SIM binding requirements for messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram take effect on January 1, 2027 . Apps will stop working unless the registered SIM is physically present and active in the phone. MediaNama is hosting an invite-only virtual discussion on whether SIM binding is technically feasible and whether it will curb fraud. The discussion will take place on November 13, from 1:30 pm to 4:30 pm. Apply to attend here . Here goes: How many child abuse ads did Meta approve in India? [ Aakriti Bansal ] Meta said on October 7 that it had added artificial intelligence (AI) tools to detect ads that covertly direct users to child sexual abuse material (CSAM) hosted on other platforms. A BBC Eye investigation had found Instagram running such paid ads in India three months earlier. Meta said it “actioned” 5.3 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content on Facebook and Instagram in India between January and June 2026. That is about 16% of the 33.2 million pieces it actioned globally. The post gave no figure for CSAM-linked ads. What we asked: We sent Meta the following questions: When did Meta deploy the new ad review measures, and does any human now review ads before they run in India? How many CSAM-linked ads did Meta find and remove in India beyond the ads the BBC reported? How many of the 5.3 million pieces of content were ads, and how many did Meta remove? Before September 2026, did Meta report CSAM found in India directly to Indian police, as the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 requires? Has Meta responded to the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology’s (MeitY) notice, and how does it respond to the first information report (FIR)? Does Meta consider itself covered by safe harbour under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act) for paid ads it approves? What they said: No response. Why it matters: Meta’s 98% figure counts the content it caught before users reported it. The figure does not cover content Meta never detected. When the BBC reported one ad in July, Instagram replied that it did not violate community standards. MeitY sources later said Meta could not rely on the third-party content defence for ads it was paid to run. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) noted that Section 79 does not absolve platforms of their duty under POCSO to report offences to the police. Meta now reports cases to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C). Before that, it sent them through the US-based National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC). Meta’s post does not say when it began reporting directly to Indian police. Who blocked NoCap’s Facebook page, and why? [ Anjali Tripathi ] Meta blocked the Facebook page of NoCap, a Malayalam digital news outlet, in India on September 28. NoCap received only an in-app notice. It cited “a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3) (b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.” The notice named no posts, no issuing authority and no reason. NoCap’s chief editor asked the Kerala High Court (HC) on October 23 to make the authorities produce the order. The petition gives these figures: Views: The page averaged 6 lakh views a day. Daily views fell to 4,538 on October 4. Earnings: Earnings between September 28 and October 20 fell by almost 91%. Income source: Facebook monetisation was NoCap’s main source of income. What we asked: We sent questions to Meta and Kerala Police. Among them: Which authority sent the notice that led to the restriction, and will Meta share it with the page’s owner? Did the notice identify specific posts, and why did Meta restrict the entire page? Did Kerala Police issue an intimation concerning NoCap’s page, and which officer issued it? Has the intimation been reviewed, as Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (IT Rules) requires every month? What they said: No response. Why it matters: On October 5, the Punjab and Haryana HC set aside a Yamuna Nagar police intimation that had restricted Haryana 24 News Network’s Facebook page. The court held that the user must get a copy of the intimation when it goes to the platform. NoCap’s petition argues that no confidentiality clause covers Section 79(3)(b). The 2009 Blocking Rules attach one only to Section 69A orders. Who tells the public when AI attacks drain Rs 300 crore from lenders? [ Azdhan ] AI-powered cyberattacks reportedly took about Rs 300 crore from smaller non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) over roughly two months. The Economic Times reported the figure, citing sources. It also reported that the attacks led to more than 150 FIRs. No regulator has published the losses. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and its financial-sector arm, CSIRT-Fin, issued a “Critical” advisory on October 9 to NBFCs, digital lenders and fintechs. The advisory describes how attackers steal payment gateway and partner-bank application programming interface (API) credentials. They use those credentials to bypass Know Your Customer (KYC) checks and per-transaction limits. The advisory names no affected entity and gives no loss figure. No Reserve Bank of India (RBI) notice does either. What we asked: We wrote to the RBI, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), CERT-In and CSIRT-Fin. Among the questions: Can the RBI confirm the Rs 300 crore estimate, and how many NBFCs have reported cyber incidents since August? Must NBFCs tell customers about cyber incidents that affect their funds or data? If not, will the RBI issue such a direction before the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules take effect? Has any listed NBFC disclosed these losses under Regulation 30 of the SEBI Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015? Will CERT-In publish aggregate, non-attributed data on incidents, losses and remediation status? What they said: No response. Why it matters: CERT-In’s 2022 directions require organisations to report a cyber incident within six hours of noticing it. The RBI’s July 2026 directions set the same deadline for NBFCs. Both require sending the report to the regulator and carry no public disclosure requirement. Three other October cases became public through media reports or leak claims before the institutions disclosed them: Central Bank of India: Its Rs 13.97 crore loss surfaced through a police complaint that Hindustan Times reported. State Bank of India (SBI): SBI disclosed the exposure of 3,897 customers’ data to stock exchanges on October 21. A threat actor had claimed to hold the data on the dark web two days earlier. CoinDCX: Its chief executive called reports of a breach a false alarm on October 22. The company admitted a Rs 152 crore loss three days later. The DPDP Rules require companies to notify affected individuals of a breach from May 13, 2027. It is unclear whether that rule covers theft of funds through payment APIs. Why did Instagram block, restore and re-block a comedian’s reel? [ Anjali Tripathi ] Instagram restricted stand-up comedian Kajol Srinivasan’s reel in India within minutes of her posting it. Instagram then restored the reel and restricted it again, according to screenshots Srinivasan shared on X on October 25. The reel was about someone using AI to summon the dead. The first notice said an automated system implemented to comply with the IT Rules had restricted access. A second notice said the government request or legal requirement behind the restriction had expired or been reversed. None of the notices named a law or an authority. What we asked: We sent questions to Meta and MeitY. Among them: Did Instagram restrict the reel following a government or law-enforcement request, and if so, which authority sent it and under which legal provision? Did Instagram apply the restriction automatically, and what triggered the restoration? Did Instagram receive a fresh request before restricting the reel again? Did MeitY or any other government authority issue a request concerning the reel? What they said: No response. Why it matters: Instagram’s notices in India cite different legal routes, and each route works differently: Section 69A: MeitY orders a block through a committee process under the 2009 Blocking Rules. Section 79(3)(b): The “appropriate Government or its agency” flags content, and the platform must act or lose its legal immunity. Cartoonist Satish Acharya received notices citing both, with two naming Section 79(3)(b) and two naming only an automated system. When Instagram restored a reel on Google’s Visakhapatnam data centre after 111 days, its panel said the restriction had ended on May 22. The restriction began on May 22. What does Meta do with the prompts users type into its algorithm? [ Prabhanu Kumar Das ] Meta announced on October 13 that it is rolling out Your Algorithm on Facebook. The tool lets users customise Feed and Reels recommendations by typing natural language prompts. It also lets users mark individual posts as ‘Interested’ or ‘Not interested’. MediaNama checked an India-based account. Neither Your Algorithm nor any similar feature is available on Facebook, Instagram or Threads in India. What we asked: We sent Meta the following questions: Which countries have access to the feature, and when will it reach India across Facebook, Instagram and Threads? How does Meta store and process the prompts and feedback, how long does it retain them, and can users view or delete their prompt history? Does Meta use these prompts and feedback to build user profiles for targeted advertising? If so, can users opt out? Does Meta use the prompts and feedback to train or fine-tune its large language models (LLMs) or other AI systems? Do any additional privacy safeguards apply to prompts that Meta’s AI systems process? What they said: No response. Why it matters: Meta said in July that it runs every public Instagram Feed and Reels post through an LLM to analyse topic and tone. It uses the results for ranking, recommendations and moderation. Its Your Algorithm announcement does not say whether user prompts feed ad targeting or model training. When MediaNama tested the similar Dear Algo feature on Threads in February with a UK account, the feed first showed the luxury posts it asked for. It then began showing posts written in Tagalog. In September, government sources said Meta cannot be treated as a “simple intermediary” because its algorithms decide what users see. articles.title: Automated Civic Alerts Provoke Concerns Over Hallucinated Public Warnings
articles.content: This story was produced by Grist and co-published with WIRED . It is part of Distorted , a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation. ​​ Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds. The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.  “That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.” Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest. . To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.  “A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don’t prioritize it until they realize they should have. They’re just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.” Emergency department personnel with the city of New York monitor the watch-command room in Brooklyn on February 23, 2026, ahead of a winter storm. Matthew Hoen / NurPhoto via Getty Images Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.  As climate disasters become more frequent and widespread, there have been numerous examples of flawed human communication scrambling an emergency response. In 2016, for instance, adjacent counties in California issued a “voluntary evacuation” and a “mandatory evacuation” for the same wildfire. In Australia in 2019, officials warned about wildfires by using the phrase “Watch and Act,” which the government later said caused “significant confusion” because no one knew what it meant. . To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How In some cases, inadequate communication can mean the difference between life and death. This happened in Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire. A few weeks after the fire, a heavy rainstorm produced a deadly mudslide. The government of Santa Barbara County struggled to communicate the risk to residents still traumatized from the blaze and  experiencing a phenomenon that Sutton calls “warning fatigue.” The county sent alerts to everyone in the “voluntary evacuation zone” for wildfires , telling residents to “stay alert to changing conditions and be prepared to leave immediately.” Most of those residents should have left immediately, but to many the evacuation notice was optional; others just didn’t want to evacuate for a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others. Governments that put out bad warnings are apt to lose the public’s trust said Sutton. “They’re losing the opportunity to be that voice to help people to be safe.” After a series of erroneous evacuation alerts to L.A. residents sparked panic during an active wildfire season in January 2025, the director of the county’s emergency management department apologized. Chris Delmas / AFP via Getty Images In theory, alerts are a perfect use case for artificial intelligence, and in particular for the generative AI systems that have developed at a dramatic pace over the past few years. FEMA provides training sessions for emergency managers to learn best practices for synthesizing and sending alerts, but many officials don’t remember all their training when an emergency arrives. A large language model is different. It can read hundreds of thousands of alerts in mere minutes, digest all the research on what works in similar scenarios, and then apply that to edit a human alert in seconds. “If you’ve only sent one [alert] in your life, and that was 15 years ago, and you need to remember all your training, and you’re thinking ‘Hey, there’s a chemical plume coming my way, the phone’s ringing, the radio’s blaring, I need help,’ the AI is probably gonna do a better job than you are,” said Rob Dale, a former meteorologist who now runs the emergency management department in Ingham County, Michigan. Dale has already used AI to draft a few practice alerts behind the scenes, but he’s never had to send one out. Ingham County is a small county in central Michigan, and it’s immune from major weather events like hurricanes and fires. If such an event did happen, Dale said he would have no issue allowing a chatbot to draft his incident communication, but he’d still want control over sending the alert out.  Some experts believe the technology is already good enough to deploy. EM1, a startup that produces AI software for emergency managers, has used Sutton’s research to train a model that its executives say is already better than almost any human emergency manager. The company has tested this in-house model on a number of scenarios including wildfires and tsunamis. It can already match or exceed human capabilities on most benchmark tests. Sutton gave Grist an example of how the software works: Grist provided her with a recent alert sent by a New Mexico county that was trying to warn residents about flooding on the San Juan River. The original alert “Breeched banks. The water is rising. EVACUATE NOW. McGee Park open for people and pets, RV.” 1 of 1 Sutton asked the EM1 model to evaluate and revise the alert. In a few seconds, it produced what she said is a far better alert, one that checks all the main boxes of disaster communication. The new alert “San Juan County: Floodwater is rising near [location]. People in [evacuation area]: LEAVE NOW for higher ground. Do not walk or drive through floodwater. McGee Park is open for people and pets. Check [official update source] for updates.” 1 of 1 The model identified and fixed several problems with the original text, which does not say who is sending the alert, name the specific location where flooding is happening, or clarify who needs to evacuate and give advice on how to do so safely. It misspells the word “breached,” and it doesn’t provide any guidance on where residents can seek further information.  EM1 has contracts with around a hundred government agencies and school districts, but none are using it to automate their extreme weather alerts just yet. For the moment, they’re only using it to workshop plans and internal preparations. Even so, all the experts interviewed for this story said they are certain that many emergency managers are already using chatbots to write messages, even if they won’t admit it. Sutton said that the emergency managers who take her alert training sessions often present her with high-quality alerts they have drafted in seconds using ChatGPT or Gemini.  “Official adoption is pretty low, but people are unofficially using it, absolutely,” said Sarah Miller, a professor of emergency management at Pierce College in Washington and a longtime instructor at the National Disaster Preparedness Training Center. “They’re using their own personal accounts, or they’re using free ones.” It sounds like an easy trade-off: if AI is better and faster than humans, and the difference between a good alert and a bad alert can be life and death, we should be using AI for every heat wave and wildfire. Yet even researchers who are bullish on chatbot technology say that making the switch could backfire. Members of the public who are skeptical of AI or who don’t trust the government in the first place may spurn agencies that publish AI-generated graphics or social media posts. In Syracuse, New York, for instance, a union of public employees sued the local government for using an AI service to answer non-emergency 911 calls.  “We trust things that we perceive [are] authentic and care about us,” said Ginny Katz, the founder of HazAdapt, a consultancy that helps disaster officials figure out how to use technology. “AI-generated content does not feel authentic.” There’s also a risk that chatbots could allow emergency managers to send out more alerts, and faster, which could increase the risk of warning fatigue. As is the case in other areas where AI is being deployed, disaster experts say that for the moment the software is only as capable as the person using it. A seasoned emergency manager might be able to speed up their communication with the public by having a chatbot draft a series of alerts, but an inexperienced one rushing to create an urgent alert won’t know how to evaluate the output of a model like ChatGPT or Claude.  Even though the technology is a ways off from being able to perform without a human expert in the loop, that hasn’t stopped many understaffed emergency management departments from using it. As for how the proliferation of AI-generated content is affecting public trust in government, experts say it’s too early to tell. “If you had a human sending you a text message versus a computer sending you a text message, which one would you believe is being more accurate?” said Justin Snair, the founder of Preppr, another company that offers AI software to emergency managers.  The answer, he said, depends on the person receiving it. articles.title: Chinese Intelligence Vessels Tracked Operating off Taiwan Waters
articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source Four Chinese survey ships spotted near Taiwan since May are suspected of gathering intelligence on undersea cables, Japanese newspaper the Yomiuri Shimbun reported yesterday, citing data from an intelligence company and Taiwanese authorities. The four ships have been spotted repeatedly making irregular moves in specific waters around Taiwan close to routes where international undersea cables connecting Taiwan and other areas have been laid, the report said. The four ships are the Xiangyang Hong 22 (向陽紅22), which belongs to the Chinese Ministry of Natural Resources; the Tongji (同濟號) and Jia Geng (嘉庚號), operated by universities in Shanghai and China’s Fujian Province, respectively; and a vessel whose Automatic Identification System (AIS) identified it as Mushanzi (暮山紫), it said. Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration via CNA The newspaper cited analysis conducted by ingeniSPACE, a geospatial intelligence analytics firm based in the US and Taiwan, using data from AIS and other sources, as well as through information obtained by the newspaper from Taiwanese authorities, it said. The Xiangyang Hong 22 has repeatedly sailed back and forth in specific waters off northern Taiwan since May, frequently slowing down, stopping and making irregular course changes, the report said, citing data provided by the company. The Jia Geng engaged in similar behavior in eastern waters, and the Mushanzi made similar moves in the Bashi Channel in the south, while the Tongji was spotted repeatedly circling Taiwan proper, and stopping and slowing down at specific locations, it said. The intelligence firm assessed that the Chinese ships have surveyed undersea cables in a wide area, identifying the routes where major undersea cables have been laid using its own method, the report said. Based on AIS data, the company concluded that the waters where the four ships slowed down or stopped all coincided with locations where undersea cables connecting Taiwan and other countries have been laid, the newspaper said. A Taiwanese official told the newspaper that the data and analysis presented by the company was deemed reliable, as they are consistent with the authorities’ understanding of the situation. Another official was quoted as saying that the possibility of Chinese survey ships collecting information on undersea cables cannot be ruled out. From 2021 through last year, Taiwan experienced a series of incidents in which undersea cables are believed to have been cut or damaged intentionally by cargo ships and other vessels, the report said. Taiwanese authorities have pointed to China’s involvement in these cases, it added. The activities of such Chinese ships could be preparation for sabotaging undersea cables, Keio University professor Motohiro Tsuchiya, an expert on issues related to undersea cables, told the newspaper, citing China’s past moves. China “may have been surveying not only the location of the cables, but also the seabed topography, water depth and ocean currents where the cables have been laid,” he was quoted as saying. Activities by Chinese vessels similar to those around Taiwan also have been observed in waters near Japan and the Philippines, ingeniSPACE’s chief operating officer Jason Wang (王柏仁) told the newspaper. In May, Japan and the Philippines agreed to start negotiations toward the delimitation of boundaries of their exclusive economic zones and continental shelves, the report said. Objecting to this move, China has repeatedly deployed patrol vessels and survey ships to waters near Taiwan, asserting what it calls “jurisdiction,” it said. China is using “gray zone” tactics in a wide area along the First Island Chain, which stretches from south of Kyushu to Taiwan and the Philippines, in anticipation of a contingency, Wang was quoted as saying. Taiwan has been cautious about the “gray zone” tactics by China, which are aimed at causing social disruption through communication outages, such as disguising cable cuts as accidents, the report said. There has also been a spate of cases in which undersea cables were cut or damaged in the Baltic Sea since 2024, with the involvement of China and Russia suspected, the report said. Undersea cables, which are used for high-capacity communications, are said to take more than a week to repair if cut in deep-sea areas, it said. SHORT-TERM OUTLOOK: The Chinese military would most likely focus on rebuilding its organization and leadership in the next few years, experts said Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) military purge has reduced the risks of a planned war against Taiwan, yet increased the danger of a conflict sparked by a miscalculation or accident, Taiwanese experts said yesterday. They made the comments at a seminar on the Fifth Plenary Session of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th Central Committee held by the research group Secure Taiwan Associate Corp (STA) in Taipei. The wholesale sacking of Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) officers and managers of the aerospace and defense industry is sure to set back Xi’s timetable to prepare the PLA to launch an invasion of Taiwan BATTLE-TESTED: Czech companies’ drones, software and navigation systems have been tested in the Ukraine war, while other countries’ are lab-tested, a Czech ex-official said Czech manufacturers are interested in setting up drone assembly lines in Taiwan, former Czech Chamber of Deputies president Marketa Pekarova Adamova told a forum in Taipei yesterday. Adamova made the comments at the inauguration of the Global UAV Academy, an organization dedicated to international cooperation in drone supply chains, technological certification and pilot training. The Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology said the Czech Republic is the largest importer of Taiwanese drones and uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) components. Adamova, who transitioned to the defense industry after retiring from politics, said the Roman adage “si vis pacem, para bellum” — “If you The husband of a Taiwanese woman stabbed to death at a hotel in Japan has been detained on suspicion of entering into a sham marriage and taking out high-value insurance policies in her name, Tainan prosecutors said today. A woman surnamed Ching (井), 38, was killed on Monday last week at a tourist hotel in Fujikawaguchiko, Japan. A Taiwanese woman surnamed Yang (楊) was arrested by Japanese police on suspicion of murder, Tainan District Prosecutors’ Office deputy chief prosecutor Wang Sheng-hao (王聖豪) said. Investigators suspect that Ching's new husband, surnamed Lee (李), 29, arranged a sham marriage, encouraged her to travel to Japan STAY VIGILANT: An aircraft carrier and battle group were located to the east of the Philippines, while other ships were identified off the east and southeast coast of Taiwan China has more than 50 naval and other official vessels operating in a wide swath of sea stretching from southern Japan down to Taiwan and off the Philippines, National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) said on Wednesday, calling the threat level “obvious.” Taiwan is stepping up efforts to issue details and maps depicting locations where Chinese warships and coast guard vessels operate. “We are staying vigilant about their activities,” Wu said. “The simultaneous threat to Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines is obvious.” The remarks accompanied a map he posted on X showing the locations of 53 ships, 34 of them navy warships,
